references.text: Jesus' parallel statement in Matthew 24:27 uses exactly the same image: just as lightning comes from the east and shines to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. This is the parallel text in Matthew's version of the end-times discourse.

In Matthew 24:30, the sign of the Son of Man in heaven and his coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory are mentioned—an elaboration on the visible and universal nature of his return, as illustrated by lightning in Luke 17:24.

The immediate context in Luke 17:22–23 warns against following those who say, 'Look here!' or 'Look there!', because the day of the Son of Man will not come secretly. The image of lightning in verse 24 explains why: his coming will be unmistakably visible to all.
In Luke 21:27, Jesus speaks of them seeing the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. This completes the picture of the visible, glorious return symbolized by lightning.

In Daniel 7:13–14, the prophet sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, and he is given dominion, glory, and a kingdom. This is the Old Testament background for the title 'Son of Man' and his glorious coming that Jesus refers to.

In Revelation 1:7, it says that he comes with the clouds, and every eye will see him. This emphasizes the universally visible nature of the Son of Man's coming, just as lightning shines from one end of heaven to the other.

In Zechariah 9:14, the Lord's lightning is described as part of his mighty revelation. The image of lightning as a sign of God's theophany and power forms the background for Jesus' use of the lightning metaphor regarding his return.

In Job 37:3, it describes how God sends his lightning across the whole sky—an image of God's majestic power shining over the entire earth, parallel to the image of the Son of Man's visible coming in Luke 17:24.

In Matthew 26:64, Jesus tells the high priest that from now on they will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven. Here too, the visible and glorious return is emphasized.

In 1 Thessalonians 5:2–3, the day of the Lord is described as coming suddenly and unexpectedly, like a thief in the night. The sudden and unavoidable aspect corresponds to the abrupt and penetrating character of lightning in Luke 17:24.
